newsitem.title: USA: Judge clears way for trial in "The Fugitive" case.
newsitem.headline: Judge clears way for trial in "The Fugitive" case.

text.p: A judge on Monday cleared the way for a trial to determine whether the wrong man was convicted more than 40 years ago in a murder case that inspired "The Fugitive" TV series and movie.

Judge Ronald Suster of the Cuyahoga County Common Pleas Court refused to dismiss a suit filed by Sam Reese Sheppard, whose father, Sam, was convicted of second degree murder in the 1954 death of his wife.
Suster rejected an argument by county prosecutors that Sheppard's estate did not have standing to pursue a wrongful imprisonment claim since the elder Sheppard is dead.

Terry Gilbert, lawyer for the younger Sheppard, told Reuters the ruling cleared the way for a trial beginning on Jan. 26, 1998, "at which time the issue before the judge will be whether or not it is more than likely that he was innocent of the charges of which he was convicted."

If the estate wins a favourable ruling it can then sue the state of Ohio for damages in another court. But Carmen Marino, first assistant Cuyahoga County prosecutor, said additional motions may be filed in the case and the January trial date may be pushed back.

The elder Sheppard was a Cleveland-area osteopath at the time his wife Marilyn, 31 and pregnant, was beaten to death on July 4, 1954, at their home in Bay Village. Her death was front-page news across the country.

Sheppard maintained until his death in 1970 that the crime was committed by a bushy-haired intruder who knocked him out. While the case inspired the "Fugitive," it carried only a loose resemblance to the fictional story of Richard Kimble.

Unlike Kimble, who escapes and finds the real killer, Sheppard did not flee custody. He was convicted within six months of the crime and spent 10 years in prison before a judge freed him saying excessive media coverage had tainted the trial.
At a second trial a jury acquitted him. He died in 1970 at the age of 46.
The younger Sheppard, who was a 7-year-old asleep at home when his mother was slain, claims that evidence may show a family employe was the real killer.

If the judge rules that Sheppard was wrongfully imprisoned the estate would be free to go to the Ohio Court of Claims to seek damages of $25,000 a year for each year Sheppard spent in prison plus economic damages and fees, Gilbert said.
